source: Chen & Klahr (1999) All other things being equal: acquisition and transfer of the control of variables strategy
finding: Children aged 7 to 10 learned CVS when given explicit training inside a domain plus probe questions. Probe questions alone, with no direct instruction, did not help. Age improved transfer to remote tasks. Trained CVS also led to better domain concepts, because unconfounded tests gave clearer data.
numbers: N = 87 children, ages 7 to 10 (abstract on PubMed PMID 10546337 and ERIC EJ597753). Per-condition mastery percentages and transfer rates were NOT read: full text is paywalled and the CMU open copy returned 404.
quote: Providing probes without direct instruction, however, did not improve children's ability to design unconfounded experiments
limits: Only the abstract was read. No cell-level numbers. The same lab later replicated it (d03).
agent_relevance: Teaching the rule plus probing works; probing alone does not. For an agent, a rule stated in the prompt matters more than a vague question such as 'is this a fair test?'.

source: Klahr & Nigam (2004) The equivalence of learning paths in early science instruction
finding: Many more third and fourth graders learned CVS from direct instruction than from discovery learning. Later, on a broader task (judging science-fair posters), the many direct-instruction learners did as well as the few discovery learners who found the method alone. So the route to learning did not matter once the skill was learned.
numbers: N = 112 third- and fourth-grade children (abstract, PubMed PMID 15447636). The widely quoted 77% vs 23% mastery figure is NOT in the abstract and could not be checked: the paper is paywalled and no open copy was found.
quote: many more children learned from direct instruction than from discovery learning
limits: Abstract only. 77% vs 23% stays unverified. One topic (ramps) and grades 3-4 only.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 is half closed: N=112 and the direction are confirmed, the headline percentages are not. Do not cite 77/23 as fact in schema notes.

source: Strand-Cary & Klahr (2008) Developing elementary science skills: instructional effectiveness and path independence
finding: Same lab, new sample. At every grade (3, 4, 5) many more children learned CVS in the explicit condition than in the exploration condition. What the child learned predicted far transfer better than how the child learned it. This repeats and extends Klahr & Nigam 2004.
numbers: N = 72 children in grades 3, 4 and 5. Transfer tested at 1 week, 3 months and 3 years (ERIC EJ819444 abstract). Condition percentages are not in the abstract.
quote: what students learned was a better predictor of far transfer than the way that they learned
limits: Abstract only. Not an independent lab.
agent_relevance: The short-run advantage of explicit teaching is replicated. For an agent, state the CVS rule in the S4 text instead of hoping the model finds it.

source: Dean & Kuhn (2007) Direct instruction vs. discovery: the long view
finding: An independent lab used the same age group and a similar design but followed children for much longer. Direct instruction was neither necessary nor sufficient for robust, lasting CVS. Skill built up gradually over many practice sessions.
numbers: Three groups of 15 fourth graders. Group 1: 12 sessions over 10 weeks of problems that need CVS. Group 2: one direct-instruction session, then the same 12 sessions. Group 3: the direct-instruction session only (ERIC EJ760016 abstract).
quote: direct instruction appears to be neither a necessary nor sufficient condition for robust acquisition
limits: Abstract only. Tiny groups. It qualifies the short-run result of Klahr & Nigam; it does not overturn it.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: a rule told once is not enough for lasting use. Repeated practice mattered. For the agent, repeat the one-change check at every test, not once at the start.

source: Lorch et al. (2010) Learning the control of variables strategy in higher and lower achieving classrooms; WWC review (2012)
finding: Large classroom trial. All three teaching conditions improved from pretest to posttest, and gains held at a 5-month delay. Order of gains: lecture plus experiments > lecture only > experiments only. Higher-achieving schools gained more in every condition. Item analysis: the lecture taught students to control irrelevant variables; hands-on experimenting taught them to vary the focal variable.
numbers: Journal abstract: n = 797 students, 36 fourth-grade classrooms. WWC review (ERIC ED535812): randomised trial, 848 students in 39 classrooms in 12 schools; meets WWC standards without reservations. The counts differ because of different analysis samples.
quote: interactive lecture improved students' understanding of the need to control irrelevant variables, and experimentation improved students' understanding of the need to vary the focal variable
limits: Abstracts only. Written test of valid vs invalid comparisons, so it measures recognising fair tests more than designing them.
agent_relevance: Two skills sit inside 'one change per test': hold the others fixed, and actually vary the focal one. An S4 check should test both halves.

source: Lorch et al. (2014) valid and invalid designs; Matlen & Klahr (2013) sequential guidance; invent-then-tell vs tell-then-practice (2017)
finding: Showing invalid (confounded) designs to explain CVS beat showing only valid designs on far transfer. High guidance in both phases beat low guidance in both phases, and starting with exploration gave no benefit. But an invent-then-tell method tied with tell-then-practice for CVS.
numbers: Lorch 2014: n = 1,069 students in 60 fourth-grade classrooms; in higher-achieving schools Invalid > Valid > Control on far transfer (EJ1054467). Matlen & Klahr 2013: N = 57 third graders, high-high beat low-low, 5-month follow-up (EJ999871). Tie study: 101 fourth and fifth graders, equal gains on immediate and far-transfer tests (EJ1157912).
limits: Abstract-level only for all three. The tie study is a partial failure to replicate 'direct instruction wins', so the effect depends on the contrast used.
agent_relevance: Showing the agent a confounded example and asking what is wrong may teach more than showing only clean examples. Cheap to test as a prompt variant.

source: ERIC EJ1039461 (2014) Children's acquisition and use of CVS: explicit and implicit guidance; ERIC EJ1386598 (2023) CVS training, N=618
finding: Task segmentation, where a multivariable task is split so children address one variable at a time in order, worked as well as direct instruction for getting children to use CVS and draw valid inferences. Both beat unguided inquiry. In a large 2023 field trial, CVS training helped planning controlled experiments and spotting confounded ones, but not identifying or interpreting controlled ones, which developed without training.
numbers: 2014: direct instruction n = 22, task structuring n = 23, control n = 22. 2023: N = 618 children aged 10-12, half randomised to CVS training, effects mostly stable at 6 months (ERIC abstracts).
limits: Abstracts only. In 2014, CVS knowledge rose equally in both guided conditions, so more practice was still needed.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S4: structuring the task so only one variable is open per step is as good as teaching the rule. That is what a 'one change per test' schema step does mechanically. Planning is the hard sub-skill; interpreting is easy.

source: Kuhn & Dean (2005) Is developing scientific thinking all about learning to control variables?
finding: Low-achieving urban sixth graders were told only to focus their inquiry on one factor. That suggestion alone significantly increased their use of controlled comparison, a strategy that looks different on the surface. The authors argue that what develops is focusing on the effect of a single factor, not a CVS rule as such. Klahr wrote a reply in the same issue.
numbers: Abstract (PubMed PMID 16262771) gives no sample size or percentages; none were read.
quote: suggestion that they focus their investigation on the role of a single factor
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: A one-line instruction to focus on one factor can be enough to trigger controlled testing. This is the cheapest S4 wording to test first.

source: Kuhn, Garcia-Mila, Zohar & Andersen (1995) Strategies of knowledge acquisition; commentary; Kuhn et al. (2000, 2008, 2009)
finding: Microgenetic study of how people coordinate theories with new evidence. Strategies varied a lot within each person and over time, which complicated a clean stage story. A commentary argued the stages were partly produced by the experimenter's questions. Later Kuhn work: school inquiry built correct additive mental models and controlled comparison; integrating several variables to predict outcomes stayed hard after three years; the joint-effect idea was learned only gradually.
numbers: 1995: 17 community-college students (ages 22-47) and 15 fourth graders (ERIC EJ518577). 2009 (PubMed PMID 19289238): 91 sixth graders, 5 sessions of multivariable prediction; collaboration helped only temporarily, feedback on wrong answers had no effect. 2008 (EJ812135): one class followed three years. No effect sizes or percentages in any abstract.
limits: Abstracts only. Exact 1995 percentages (for example the share keeping a disconfirmed theory) were not read. No formal failed replication found, but the 1995 stage claims drew a published critique (ERIC EJ518579).
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays partly open. For the agent: expect strategy mixing inside one run; do not assume a fixed testing style.

source: Klahr & Chen (2003) Overcoming the positive-capture strategy in young children: learning about indeterminacy
finding: Four- and five-year-olds tend to treat one positive instance as proof even when another source of evidence is unexplored. This strategy is entrenched, but a few training sessions replaced it with the correct one.
numbers: Two experiments, ages 4-5; sample size not in the abstract (PubMed PMID 14552398).
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Matches the agent failure of calling a confounded result conclusive. A short trained check for 'what else changed?' is learnable.

source: Bramley, Jones, Gureckis & Ruggeri (2022) Children's failure to control variables may reflect adaptive decision-making (re-opened)
finding: On a box of switches, children chose tests to match how many switches likely worked. When one switch was expected to work (sparse), more children tested several switches at once; when many were expected (dense), more tested one at a time. Older children moved from one-at-a-time toward multi-switch tests, and older multi-switch testers were far more accurate.
numbers: N = 104 (53 aged 7-9, 51 aged 10-13). First test used multiple switches: 37.5% younger sparse, 20.7% younger dense, 60.7% older sparse, 39.1% older dense. Strategy analysis on 92 children: older less likely to test one at a time (OR 0.45, BF 2.95); dense raised test-one (OR 2.41, BF 4.33). Older test-multiple children found the correct switch 17/19 (89%) vs younger 3/7 (43%), p = .003; sparse only: 15/15 vs 2/6. Success: sparse 13/21 younger, 23/26 older; dense 16/25 younger, 10/20 older; chance 1/6.
quote: children's tendency to test multiple variables should not be taken as evidence that they are poor active learners
limits: Museum sample, one box, paid reward. The first-test condition effect was modest (BF 2.34). One lab.
agent_relevance: This is the shape of item set gap 1 asks for: a switch box where the best rule flips with sparsity. An S4 that always says 'one change per test' would be wrong on sparse boxes. Make the rule depend on how many causes are plausible.

source: Moeller, Sodian & Sobel (2022) Developmental trajectories in diagnostic reasoning (re-read for the choice/inference question)
finding: Three- to six-year-olds showed some ability to recognise confounded evidence and performed above chance in some tasks that required choosing a controlled test. But the two abilities were unrelated, so early choice of controlled tests may not come from understanding that confounded evidence blocks a conclusion.
numbers: N = 57 children aged 3 to 6. Children said they could not be sure on 39% of confounded-evidence trials. Performance on the two-variable CVS trial was negatively correlated with age (younger children more often correct).
limits: Knowledge-lean forced-choice tasks. Above chance only in some tasks. Gap 10's premise needs correcting: Moeller does not show 'recognise but cannot choose'. It shows both partly present and uncorrelated.
agent_relevance: Do not assume an agent that can label a test confounded will also choose clean tests; test each separately.

source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup, Richards, Fergus & Marino (2025) Language agents mirror human causal reasoning biases (COLM 2025)
finding: LLM agents played a text Blicket game, adding or removing one object per step, then said which objects work. They did well when any one object could trigger the machine (OR rule) and poorly when objects had to act together (AND rule). More objects (8 vs 4) made it worse. An information-gain oracle solved every case, so the AND rule was not intrinsically harder. Giving models the oracle's data helped but did not close the gap. Higher reasoning effort in o-mini models made conjunctive exploration worse. A test-time method that samples many hypotheses and eliminates them removed the OR/AND gap.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-chat, DeepSeek-reasoner, o-mini variants; 4 and 8 object settings. Oracle Q&A accuracy 1.0 on both rules. Hypothesis sampling: accuracy rose as initial unique hypotheses grew from 16 to 96, with no OR/AND decrease. Per-model Q&A percentages are in figures only.
quote: models reliably infer the common, intuitive disjunctive causal relationships but systematically struggle with the unusual
limits: Exact per-model numbers not recoverable from the text dump. Reasoning-effort result is from an appendix on the o-mini series only.
agent_relevance: First LLM evidence that a one-object-per-step interface has a boundary: with joint causes, single-object tests cannot decide, and models prefer the simple OR story. Supports listing candidate causes and hypotheses before choosing tests. Also warns that more thinking can entrench the prior.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists (full text re-read for gaps 1 and 8)
finding: Adults who chose their own tests handled conjunctive rules well. People who proposed tests but saw outcomes of someone else's tests did worst. In conjunctive worlds, successful agents moved from one-object to two-object tests, because a single-object test cannot rule out the partner. In disjunctive worlds, one- or two-object tests were enough. Six LLMs got the same action space; they did not reliably gain from choosing their own tests and lagged the best humans on conjunctive rules.
numbers: 306 adults, 102 per group (active, passive observer, passive proposer), 51 conjunctive and 51 disjunctive per group. Conjunctive object identification: active 0.69, observer 0.45, proposer 0.12. Rule inference: active 0.82, observer 0.69, proposer 0.57. Average human tests 9.6 (conjunctive) vs 6.4 (disjunctive). LLM tests (conj/disj): gpt-5 10.2/7.7, gemini-2.5-flash 13.5/9.7, o4-mini 6.7/4.2, deepseek-chat 12.3/11.9. 48 trials per model at temperature 0, 288 LLM trials.
quote: Passive Proposers performed substantially worse on object identification accuracy (0.12)
limits: The proposer group saw outcomes of a matched other person's tests, not outcomes of its own pre-written batch. So it does not test 'write a batch, then see results'. Four-object task with a 32-hypothesis space. CogSci paper, one lab.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 answer: tying the next test to the outcome of the previous one matters a lot. An S4 that writes several tests up front and runs them without updating copies the proposer condition. Keep it sequential: choose, run, update, choose.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, appendix tables re-read for non-thinking models and token cost
finding: Opposites-style prompting (Think-in-Opposites, TiO) lifts rule discovery for thinking-mode models, but for non-thinking instruct models the effect is small or mixed and the authors report no significant change. The Dual-Goal prompt tended to hurt non-thinking models. The thinking-mode gain costs about 40% more tokens per turn.
numbers: Non-thinking task success, baseline / TiO / Dual-Goal: Qwen3-8B 0.06 / 0.06 / 0.08; Qwen3-14B 0.23 / 0.29 / 0.13; Qwen3-32B 0.33 / 0.36 / 0.10; Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct 0.21 / 0.38 / 0.20. Thinking-mode baseline to TiO (cells matched to Table 2 by turn counts): Qwen3-8B 0.21 to 0.40; Qwen3-14B 0.34 to 0.58; Qwen3-32B 0.41 to 0.60; DeepSeek-R1-Llama-70B 0.35 to 0.50. Tokens per turn: non-thinking about 7 to 15 (cap 256); thinking about 1,000 to 2,300 (cap 16K). Qwen3-32B thinking: 1,030 tokens per turn baseline vs 1,450 with TiO. 80 episodes per cell.
limits: The text dump interleaves row labels in the thinking-mode table, so a few thinking cells were matched by turn count and may be swapped with Dual-Goal. Non-thinking numbers are clean. No pretrained base (non-instruct) model was tested. One lab.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 answer: no replication on a base model. On instruct non-thinking models the opposites prompt costs almost no tokens but gains are inconsistent (0 to +17 points). On small models, switching to thinking mode raised success more than any prompt. Do not count on a counterexample prompt in a cheap, no-thinking pass.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori & Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench (read for relation to Jhaveri)
finding: A different lab, a different benchmark, a semantic rule instead of number triples. It does not replicate Jhaveri's prompt interventions, because it tests none. It argues that the Jhaveri setup ignores the Klayman and Ha (1987) framework. Reasoning models generally succeed more and test negatively more than instruction-tuned models, except at the smallest scales.
numbers: Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, other instruction-tuned 33-35%, GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Positive-test share: GPT-5-Mini 39.0%, GPT-5.2-Chat 27.3%, GPT-OSS-20B 24.2%, instruction-tuned 66-82%. Conclusive falsification rate: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%, GPT-5-Nano 26.6%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%.
limits: Single task type (rule-discovery games). The first 100,000 characters of the page were read. No prompt-level intervention to compare.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 answer: a second lab echoes the bias finding (confirming tests, reasoning models better), but the specific 42% to 56% intervention effect has no independent replication. Neither paper tests tasks beyond rule discovery, except Jhaveri's Blicket distillation.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le & Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning
finding: An LLM plus Monte Carlo belief updating chooses experiments by expected information gain on a Zendo-style rule game. The authors report that LLMs are good at proposing and revising hypotheses but do not consistently beat random guessing when proposing experiments.
numbers: Zendo accuracy: average human 5.26 of 8, ReAct-style LLM agent 4.60 of 8, fuzzy-rule model 5.35 of 8, strongest model 6.55 of 8. Human data from Bramley et al.
limits: Rule-learning game, not a CVS item. The model is a scaffold with external inference, not a plain LLM.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the weak point is test choice, not hypothesis generation. A scaffold that scores candidate tests by how well they split the remaining hypotheses, in an outcome-aware loop, beat a plain agent and passed average human accuracy.

source: Chen et al. (2026) ACED-Bench; Witness (2026); SciGame (2026); DiG-bench (2026); abstract-level reads
finding: ACED-Bench evidence-ledger analysis finds agents test the wrong intervention, lose relevant evidence, or keep going after they have enough. Witness, SciGame and DiG-bench test rule inference by interaction, but none frames its tasks as controlling variables or as keeping vs dropping a disconfirmed hypothesis.
numbers: ACED-CORE 180 tasks (60 set-valued, 120 decision), ACED-QUAL 150 questions, 9 models, 3 agent designs. Witness: best of 18 models solves 24% of private slots. DiG-bench: 70 games, 7 tiers, 21 public. SciGame: 5 frontier models; familiar priors hurt once the relation is altered.
limits: Abstract pages only; no per-model scores for ACED. Loosely related to gap 6.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly: published failure modes (wrong intervention, lost evidence, no stopping) are what an S4 plus an evidence ledger targets. No study measures 'keeps a disconfirmed theory' in Kuhn's multi-session sense.

source: Absence check for LLM and CVS or MicroDYN studies (gaps 3 and 9)
finding: Searched ERIC (education), Europe PMC (including preprints), PubMed and Semantic Scholar citation lists for LLM or ChatGPT combined with control of variables, VOTAT, MicroDYN, confounded experiments and complex problem solving. Nothing relevant turned up. Citing papers of Jhaveri (9) and FalsifyBench (2) were listed; none tests CVS items. arXiv's own search was rate-limited, so coverage of very recent preprints is incomplete.
numbers: Zero studies found for LLM plus CVS on developmental items and zero for LLM plus MicroDYN. The ERIC MicroDYN query returned 3 unrelated hits.
limits: Absence of evidence under a rate-limited search; an arXiv title search could still find one. Treat as probable, not proven.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 9 stay open. The CVS item set (ramps, springs, balls, switch box) is still the missing measurement. Building it is cheaper than searching further.

source: Coenen, Ruggeri, Bramley & Gureckis (2019) Testing one or multiple (adult baseline, seen through Bramley 2022)
finding: Adults also adjust between testing one switch and testing several, depending on how many causes they expect. Bramley et al. used a 66 percentage point strategy difference between sparsity conditions in adults as the benchmark for their power analysis.
numbers: 66 percentage point difference in strategy between sparse and dense conditions in adults (as cited by Bramley et al. 2022); children were powered for 40 points.
limits: Seen through Bramley's methods text, not the original paper.
agent_relevance: Adaptive choice between single and grouped tests happens without teaching, so a schema step asking 'how many causes are plausible?' asks for a natural move.
